title: The 10 Cheapest New Trucks in America for 2026 (And the Traps Inside the Price)

scenes.text: The average full-size pickup in America now sells for more than sixty-seven thousand dollars. But there are still new trucks you can buy for under thirty thousand. One of the cheapest full-size trucks on the list is no longer being built at all. Another gets cheaper when you choose the bigger bed. And a startup says it will undercut every one of them. These are the cheapest new trucks in America, and the traps hidden inside the low prices.
scenes.caption: THE CHEAPEST NEW TRUCKS IN AMERICA

scenes.text: We ranked the ten cheapest new pickups using starting prices from Cars dot com, as of August twenty twenty-six, including the destination fee. That fee is not optional, so it belongs in the price. We will show you what you actually get at the bottom of each lineup, and which cheap trucks are a real deal and which are just bait.
scenes.caption: 10 TRUCKS, REAL PRICES

scenes.text: Every number in this video comes from a published source, listed in the description. Prices change often, so always check before you buy. If we could not confirm a figure, we left it out. Let's start with the context that makes these prices matter.
scenes.caption: EVERY NUMBER IS SOURCED

scenes.text: According to Kelley Blue Book data from Cox Automotive, the average transaction price for a full-size pickup in September twenty twenty-six was sixty-seven thousand, five hundred seventy-three dollars. Small and midsize pickups averaged forty-three thousand, seven hundred ninety. The average new vehicle of any kind sold for fifty thousand, five hundred sixty-two. So most truck buyers are paying far above the prices you are about to see.
scenes.caption: AVG FULL-SIZE: $67,573

scenes.text: Why the gap? Because the cheapest trucks are basic versions that dealers often do not stock in large numbers. Most trucks on the lot are higher trims, with bigger cabs, four-wheel drive and more features. Finding the base price often takes patience, a factory order, or a willingness to drive to another dealer. Keep that in mind as we go through the list.
scenes.caption: THE BASE TRUCK IS HARD TO FIND

scenes.text: Number ten is the G M C Sierra fifteen hundred Pro, at forty-one thousand and ninety-five dollars, according to Cars dot com. It is a regular cab with a six and a half foot bed. It is rated at twenty-five miles per gallon combined with rear-wheel drive, and up to nine thousand pounds of towing in Cars dot com's table.
scenes.caption: 10. GMC SIERRA PRO: $41,095

scenes.text: And here is the first twist. According to Cars dot com, the regular cab Sierra Pro is no longer in production. What you find is dealer stock that is still on lots. So the cheapest G M C full-size truck is a truck that is already gone from the factory. If you want one, you are buying from a shrinking supply, which can be good for negotiating, or frustrating if your dealer has none.
scenes.caption: TWIST: NO LONGER IN PRODUCTION

scenes.text: What do you give up at this price? A regular cab means two or three seats and no back seat. Base trucks usually have cloth or vinyl seats, a smaller screen, steel wheels and fewer driver assistance features. For a work truck, that is fine. For a family vehicle, it usually is not. Know what the base truck really includes before you get excited about the price.
scenes.caption: WHAT YOU GIVE UP

scenes.text: Number nine is the G M C Canyon Elevation, at forty thousand, nine hundred ninety-five dollars. Interesting fact: G M C does not offer a basic work truck version of the Canyon, so the entry model is already fairly well equipped. It has a crew cab, a five foot bed, and a two point seven liter turbo four with three hundred ten horsepower. Cars dot com lists it at twenty miles per gallon combined.
scenes.caption: 9. GMC CANYON: $40,995

scenes.text: Here is the twist. The Canyon is a midsize truck, and yet it costs almost the same as the full-size Sierra Pro and more than the full-size F-one-fifty X L. G M C positions the Canyon as a premium product, so its starting point is high. If price is what matters most, its Chevrolet twin, the Colorado, starts thousands of dollars lower.
scenes.caption: MIDSIZE, FULL-SIZE PRICE

scenes.text: Number eight is the Ford F-one-fifty X L, at forty thousand and eighty-five dollars, according to Cars dot com. This is the base version of the best-selling truck line in America. It is a regular cab, and the price is for the eight foot bed. Cars dot com lists the base two point seven liter engine at up to eight thousand four hundred pounds of towing in its text.
scenes.caption: 8. FORD F-150 XL: $40,085

scenes.text: And here is the strangest twist on the list. According to Cars dot com, the eight foot box is cheaper than the six and a half foot option. You get more truck for less money. It sounds backwards, but it reflects how Ford builds and packages its base trucks. If you need a work truck and have the room to park it, the long bed is the bargain.
scenes.caption: TWIST: BIGGER BED, LOWER PRICE

scenes.text: There is also a towing detail worth noting. Cars dot com's table and its text give different towing numbers for some trucks, because towing depends on the exact engine, axle and package. That is true for every truck on this list. Never trust a maximum towing number in an ad. Ask for the rating of the exact truck you are buying, written down.
scenes.caption: ASK FOR THE EXACT TOW RATING

scenes.text: Number seven is the Chevrolet Silverado fifteen hundred W T, for work truck, at thirty-nine thousand, six hundred ninety-five dollars. It is the cheapest full-size truck on the list. A regular cab with a six and a half foot bed and up to nine thousand one hundred pounds of towing, according to Cars dot com's table.
scenes.caption: 7. SILVERADO WT: $39,695

scenes.text: But it carries the same twist as the Sierra. According to Cars dot com, regular cab production has ended, and only dealer stock remains. So the cheapest full-size pickup in America, at least on paper, is a truck you can no longer order from the factory. When that stock is gone, the cheapest full-size truck will likely cost more.
scenes.caption: ONLY DEALER STOCK REMAINS

scenes.text: This is a bigger story than one truck. The regular cab, the simplest pickup layout, is disappearing. Most buyers want a crew cab for passengers, and carmakers build what sells. But for work fleets and budget buyers, the regular cab was the entry door. As it disappears, the starting price of a full-size truck rises with it.
scenes.caption: THE REGULAR CAB IS DISAPPEARING

scenes.text: Here is the strategy many fleet buyers use. When a regular cab is being discontinued, dealers want to clear the remaining trucks. That can mean extra discounts on top of the already low price. If you need a simple two-seat work truck, ask dealers how many leftover regular cabs they have, and how long they have been on the lot.
scenes.caption: LEFTOVERS CAN MEAN DISCOUNTS

scenes.text: Now the midsize trucks, where the real bargains start. Number six is the Ford Ranger X L, at thirty-five thousand, four hundred forty-five dollars. It has a crew cab, a five foot bed, and a two point three liter turbo four with two hundred seventy horsepower and a ten-speed automatic, according to Cars dot com.
scenes.caption: 6. FORD RANGER XL: $35,445

scenes.text: And the Ranger is on a roll. According to Ford, it sold seventy thousand, nine hundred sixty units in twenty twenty-five, up fifty-three point six percent. Here is the twist: the base Ranger comes as a crew cab, so even the cheapest version seats five. That is something no base full-size truck on this list offers at this price.
scenes.caption: 2025: +53.6% SALES

scenes.text: The Ranger is also a reminder of how much midsize trucks have grown. According to Hagerty, old compact trucks were nearly a foot shorter, about eight inches narrower and roughly a thousand pounds lighter than today's so-called small pickups. The Ranger you buy today is closer in size to a full-size truck from decades ago than to the Ranger many people remember.
scenes.caption: TODAY'S RANGER IS BIG

scenes.text: Number five is the Chevrolet Colorado W T, at thirty-four thousand, four hundred ninety-five dollars. It has a crew cab, a five foot one inch bed, and the same two point seven liter turbo four as the Canyon, with three hundred ten horsepower. Cars dot com says it can tow seven thousand seven hundred pounds when properly equipped.
scenes.caption: 5. COLORADO WT: $34,495

scenes.text: Here is the twist. The Colorado and the Canyon are close cousins, built on the same platform with the same base engine. Yet the cheapest Colorado costs six thousand five hundred dollars less than the cheapest Canyon. It is one of the clearest examples of badge pricing in the truck world. If you can live with fewer features and a Chevy badge, that difference stays in your pocket.
scenes.caption: SAME ENGINE, $6,500 LESS

scenes.text: Number four is the Toyota Tacoma S R, at thirty-four thousand, two hundred ninety dollars. It is an extended cab with a six foot bed, and a two point four liter turbo four with two hundred twenty-eight horsepower. Cars dot com lists twenty-three miles per gallon combined with rear-wheel drive.
scenes.caption: 4. TACOMA SR: $34,290

scenes.text: The Tacoma is the most popular midsize truck in America. According to Pedal Commander, it sold two hundred seventy-four thousand, six hundred thirty-eight units in twenty twenty-five, up more than forty-two percent. And according to SlashGear, J D Power has called it the most reliable midsize truck on the market. Here is the twist: the base engine in the cheapest Tacoma makes far less power than the version in higher trims. Test drive the exact truck you plan to buy.
scenes.caption: TACOMA: 274,638 SOLD IN 2025

scenes.text: Reliability matters even more on a budget truck. A cheap truck that needs expensive repairs stops being cheap very quickly. That is one reason the Tacoma holds its value so well. If you plan to keep a truck for ten years or more, a slightly higher price for a truck with a strong reliability record can save money in the long run.
scenes.caption: CHEAP TO BUY VS CHEAP TO OWN

scenes.text: Number three is the Nissan Frontier S, at thirty-three thousand, eight hundred ninety-five dollars. And it might be the best value on the whole list. According to Cars dot com, it comes with a three point eight liter V six making three hundred ten horsepower as standard, rear-wheel drive, and a six foot bed on the King Cab.
scenes.caption: 3. NISSAN FRONTIER S: $33,895

scenes.text: Here is the twist. In a market where almost every base truck has a small turbo four, the cheapest Frontier still has a naturally aspirated V six. SlashGear quoted Road and Track calling its approach a blast from the past. Cars dot com lists up to seven thousand one hundred sixty pounds of towing in its table. For buyers who want a simple, proven engine, the Frontier is one of the last of its kind.
scenes.caption: STANDARD V6: 310 HP

scenes.text: And there is another twist. Nissan gave up on its full-size Titan, which ended production in twenty twenty-four after sales fell to just fifteen thousand and sixty-three in twenty twenty-two, according to Motor Authority. But the Frontier survived. Nissan found its place in the truck market not by fighting Ford, Chevy and Ram head on, but by offering value one size down.
scenes.caption: THE TITAN DIED, THE FRONTIER LIVED

scenes.text: Number two is the Hyundai Santa Cruz S E, at thirty-one thousand, three hundred fifty dollars. It is based on the Hyundai Tucson S U V, with a crew cab, a four foot bed, and a one hundred ninety-one horsepower two point five liter four cylinder. Cars dot com lists twenty-five miles per gallon combined with front-wheel drive.
scenes.caption: 2. SANTA CRUZ SE: $31,350

scenes.text: But there is a warning. According to The Autopian in January twenty twenty-six, Automotive News reported, citing unnamed sources, that Hyundai plans to end Santa Cruz production early. Hyundai declined to confirm. The truck sold twenty-five thousand, four hundred ninety-nine units in twenty twenty-five, and the Maverick outsold it six to one. A cheap truck that might be discontinued can be a great deal, or a resale headache.
scenes.caption: WARNING: MAY END EARLY

scenes.text: Before we reveal number one, here is a question many buyers ask: is a car-based truck a real truck? The Santa Cruz and the Maverick are built like crossovers, not on a separate frame. That means a smoother ride and better fuel economy, but less towing and payload than a body-on-frame truck. For most people who haul furniture, mulch or bikes, that trade is worth it.
scenes.caption: IS IT A REAL TRUCK?

scenes.text: And number one, the cheapest new pickup in America, is the Ford Maverick X L, at twenty-eight thousand, nine hundred ninety dollars including destination, according to Cars dot com. It has a crew cab, a four and a half foot bed, and seats five. For twenty twenty-six, the base engine is a two liter turbo four, and front-wheel drive is available.
scenes.caption: 1. FORD MAVERICK XL: $28,990

scenes.text: It is also one of the best-selling small trucks in the country. According to Ford, the Maverick sold one hundred fifty-five thousand and fifty-one units in twenty twenty-five. The Maverick hybrid alone sold eighty-one thousand and thirty-four. The cheapest truck in America is not a compromise nobody wants. It is a hit.
scenes.caption: 2025: 155,051 MAVERICKS

scenes.text: Now the twist, and it matters for twenty twenty-seven. According to Ford Authority, for the twenty twenty-seven model year, the base Maverick X L becomes hybrid only. The cheapest EcoBoost model becomes the X L T all-wheel drive, at thirty thousand, seven hundred forty-five dollars, which Ford Authority says is three thousand six hundred dollars more than the cheapest twenty twenty-six gas model. The entry price of the cheapest truck may be moving.
scenes.caption: 2027: XL GOES HYBRID-ONLY

scenes.text: And here is the bigger picture. When the Maverick launched for twenty twenty-two, it started under twenty thousand dollars before destination. Today, the cheapest one costs about twenty-nine thousand with destination. Even the cheapest truck in America has climbed by thousands of dollars in just a few years.
scenes.caption: FROM UNDER $20K TO ~$29K

scenes.text: So is anything cheaper coming? Yes, at least on paper. According to The Next Web, in June twenty twenty-six, the startup Slate Auto opened preorders for a small, two-seat electric pickup starting at twenty-four thousand nine hundred fifty dollars. More than one hundred eighty thousand reservations were converted into three hundred dollar nonrefundable deposits.
scenes.caption: SLATE: $24,950 EV PICKUP

scenes.text: It would be the cheapest new pickup in America by about four thousand dollars. But here is the twist. According to The Next Web, Slate still needs federal vehicle validation and certification before it can legally deliver trucks, and it had not disclosed its status. Deliveries were expected in the fourth quarter of twenty twenty-six. Until trucks reach customers, it is a promise, not a price you can pay.
scenes.caption: TWIST: NOT YET CERTIFIED

scenes.text: And there is a used-truck angle. When new truck prices climb, many buyers turn to used trucks. A two or three year old midsize truck can sometimes cost less than a new base model while offering a higher trim. But used truck prices also rose in recent years, so always compare the full cost, including interest rates, which are often higher for used vehicles.
scenes.caption: THE USED-TRUCK ANGLE

scenes.text: So what does the list tell us? First, the cheapest trucks in America are small and midsize. Six of the ten cheapest are midsize or compact, and the cheapest full-size trucks start around forty thousand. Second, the cheapest full-size trucks are disappearing, as regular cab production ends. And third, the gap between the cheapest truck and the average truck is huge.
scenes.query: Ford Maverick Nissan Frontier Toyota Tacoma
scenes.caption: WHAT THE LIST TELLS US

scenes.text: And the final twist. In nineteen twenty-five, according to The Henry Ford, Ford's Model T pickup cost two hundred eighty-one dollars, and it was built so working people could afford it. One hundred years later, the cheapest pickup costs about twenty-nine thousand. The idea of the affordable truck is not dead. But it is fighting for space in a market built around sixty-seven thousand dollar trucks.
scenes.caption: $281 IN 1925

scenes.text: So how do you actually get a cheap truck in twenty twenty-seven? First, always compare prices including destination. A low headline price can hide a two to three thousand dollar fee. Second, ask about factory orders. If the base truck is not on the lot, ordering it can be the only way to pay the base price.
scenes.caption: CHECKS 1 AND 2: DESTINATION, ORDER
scenes.chapter: What to check before you buy in 2027

scenes.text: Third, check whether the model is still in production. Leftover regular cab trucks can be bargains, but discontinued models can lose value faster. Fourth, compare twins like the Colorado and Canyon, where the same engineering can cost thousands less. And fifth, count the full cost: fuel, insurance and resale value. The Maverick hybrid, for example, can save a lot of fuel compared with a bigger truck.
scenes.caption: CHECKS 3, 4 AND 5

scenes.text: We put all of these checks into the Twenty Twenty-Seven Truck Buyer's Guide, with the numbers to compare and the questions to ask every dealer. The link is in the description and in the pinned comment. Subscribe for the next video, about five trucks that became collectibles. And tell us in the comments: which cheap truck would you buy? Thanks for watching.
